props.title: Rita, Sue and Bob Too
props.initialSlug: Bradford teens affair with married man

sections.content: Alan Clarke's Rita, Sue and Bob Too (1987) stands as a raw, unflinching portrait of working-class British life that shocked audiences with its frank depiction of sexuality and poverty. Set against the backdrop of Bradford's council estates, the film follows two teenage babysitters who begin an affair with a married man, combining dark humor with social commentary in ways that echo other British kitchen sink dramas like The Long Good Friday (1980) and Mona Lisa (1986). The film's controversial themes and explicit content caused significant debate upon release, yet its honest portrayal of class dynamics and teenage sexuality remains influential in British cinema.

sections.content: Director Alan Clarke established himself as a fearless chronicler of Britain's underclass through works like Made in Britain (1982) and Scum (1979). His documentary-style approach in Rita, Sue and Bob Too creates an uncomfortable intimacy that forces viewers to confront social issues without moral judgment. The film shares DNA with later working-class narratives like Trainspotting (1996) and Fish Tank (2009), maintaining a tradition of British cinema that refuses to look away from societal difficulties.

The film's treatment of teenage sexuality proved especially controversial, yet its frank approach influenced later British coming-of-age films like Beautiful Thing (1996) and Me Without You (2001). Writer Andrea Dunbar drew from her own experiences growing up on Bradford's Buttershaw estate, lending the screenplay an authenticity that cuts through potential exploitation. sections.content: Rita, Sue and Bob Too exists within a crucial lineage of British social realist cinema, connecting the angry young men of the 1960s like This Sporting Life (1963) with contemporary directors like Ken Loach and Andrea Arnold. Its mix of comedy and social commentary influenced films like East is East (1999) and The Full Monty (1997), showing how humor can make difficult subjects more accessible without diminishing their impact.
